name: Rafael Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Rafael. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a transmission crew, the big towers, the lines that carry power from the dam down to the city. Most days we drive out from the yard by the reservoir before sunrise, do the safety briefing at the base of the tower, and then we're up there replacing insulator strings or spacers, sixty metres off the ground. I like the quiet up there, honestly, and I like that my crew trusts me to call it if the wind gets up. What wears me out is the driving, two hours each way some days on gravel roads.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has the job changed much in your time?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot, and mostly for the better. When I started we walked the lines with binoculars, and now the company flies drones and we get photos of every bolt before we climb. I was against it at first, I thought it was a way to cut jobs, but it turned out it just meant we climbed the right tower first. I use one of those AI chat programs now and then, mainly when we get a manual in German for new tensioning gear or I need help writing up an incident report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the things that actually matter, like pay and staffing. At the yard we'd joke about the consultants who sold the bosses on robots. I'd probably put something on the union page about putting the money into people instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life carries on, and I'm fine with that. The trouble is we're always one bad month away from trouble, and that has nothing to do with AI. Lucia and I are still helping Javi with his studies and the car needs work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I am and keep using the AI thing for manuals, since it's handy. I'd push for a proper raise at the next round. I might ask about the tower rescue instructor role, which pays a bit more, because I've got eight years left and it'd boost the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, because the money worry doesn't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay is the real issue. What would you want from the next deal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're paid less than the crews at the bigger company two valleys over, and it shows when you fill the tank. I'd want the remote-site allowance raised and a pension top-up for the people who stay past 55. That's what keeps good people climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner make of all this AI talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia works nights at a care home and she laughs at it. She says the day a robot can turn an old man in his bed gently, she'll start worrying. She's probably right, but I tell her not to say that too loud.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about what matters, like pay and staffing. I'd post on the union page about putting money into people instead of gadgets.
S0.think: Privately, my life carries on and I'm fine with that. The real problem is being one bad month away from trouble, which has nothing to do with AI.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps using AI for translating manuals. Pushes for a raise at the next pay round and asks about a better-paid tower rescue instructor role to boost his pension.
S0.feel: Calm, but a little flat because the money worry stays.
S0.quote: She says the day a robot can turn an old man in his bed gently, she'll start worrying.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is relaxed about AI as a tool because he watched drones turn out well. His stress is purely financial and long-standing. He thinks about the pension in concrete steps, like the instructor role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a deal now, before the machines arrive, not after. At work I'd tell the younger guys to get their names down for whatever training comes. Online I'd back the union's push for a public retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out fine if I play it right. They'll need someone who knows the lines to run the machines, and I've been doing that with drones for years. But I'm also the expensive one at 58, and that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the new kit is proven on a real job, then put my hand up first to learn it. In the first year I'd do whatever courses the company offers and try to get on the trial crew. I'd also try to clear the car loan early so we've got a little breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. More like when a new boss starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned drones that can string line. Have you actually seen that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At a trade show two years back, yes. A drone pulled a pilot rope between two towers in about ten minutes, a job that takes us half a day with a helicopter. It was impressive and it made my stomach turn a bit, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The training, fully, in work hours, not on our own time. And a promise that if a crew shrinks, the older ones get a fair early exit and the younger ones get kept on. That's how you do it properly.

S1.say: I'd say we need a deal now, before the machines arrive. I'd tell the younger crew to sign up for training and back the union's push for a public retraining fund.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd come out fine if I play it right, because they'll need people who know the lines to run the machines. But at 58 I'm the expensive one, and that worries me.
S1.do: Waits until new equipment is proven, then volunteers first to learn it and joins a trial crew. Takes company courses in the first year and tries to pay off the car loan early.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, like when a new boss starts.
S1.quote: It was impressive and it made my stomach turn a bit, both at once.
S1.fieldNote: His steady style is clear: he won't jump first, but once something is proven he wants to be first in line. He supports public schemes and a negotiated deal. His worry about being the expensive older worker sits just under the confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three are about full AGI, at different speeds. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has failed us if it lets this happen with no plan. I'd be at every union meeting saying we need income support and a slowdown on the grid until there's a plan. And I'd say it online too, which I don't usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm likely finished before I'm ready. Two years puts me at 60, with maybe four weeks of money in the bank and no other transmission work within a day's drive. If a robot can climb the tower and do the job, there's no reason for them to keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away: no holiday, sell the second car, tell Javi we can't help with fees next year. I'd sign up for every union action going. I'd also look at whether Lucia could pick up more shifts, since care work might last longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. A cold feeling, like when someone on your crew slips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Neil, who's 52 and has a disabled son. He's the kind who'd keep quiet and just go under. And our young guy Tomas, who just bought a house on the strength of this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to be first to learn new kit. Does that still hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, but I'd be honest that it's probably pointless. In two years there wouldn't be time for anything to be proven, so I'd be learning to run something that might replace the person running it too. I'd do it anyway, because doing nothing is worse.

S2.say: I'd say the government has failed if it lets this happen with no plan. I'd push at union meetings and online for income support and a slowdown until there's a plan.
S2.think: Privately I think I'm likely finished at 60, with maybe four weeks of money and no other transmission work nearby. If a robot can do the tower work, there's no reason to keep me.
S2.do: Cuts spending straight away, skips the holiday, sells the second car and stops helping with his son's fees. Joins every union action, tries to learn new kit anyway, and looks at his partner taking more shifts.
S2.feel: Scared, with a cold feeling like seeing someone on his crew slip.
S2.quote: I'd be learning to run something that might replace the person running it too.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline breaks his usual approach of waiting for proof, and he knows it. He still chooses to try rather than freeze. His worry spreads quickly to named crew members, Neil and Tomas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them: a plan for every worker, paid for by the companies that profit. I'd say it at the union branch and I'd write to my representative. I'd say it calmer than with the fast one, but I'd keep saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tight but I could make it. In five years I'd be 63, and if I've moved into running and checking the machines by then, I might hang on till my pension. If not, it's a short gap to bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into the trial crew as soon as the robots were proven and get qualified on them in the first couple of years. I'd put something aside every month, even a small amount, and pay off the car. I'd also push the union for a bridge to the pension for anyone over 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a worry I can do something with. The two-year one felt like falling; this feels like climbing in bad weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do this month if you knew this was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Lucia and do a proper budget, which we've never really done. Then ask my supervisor straight out what the company's plans are. Better to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you encourage your sons to do anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo's a welder, so I'd tell him to get onto whatever's building or fixing the robots. Javi's studying environmental science, which I think might hold up. I'd tell them both not to wait for things to be proven like their dad does.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them for a plan for every worker, paid for by the companies that profit. I'd raise it at the union branch and write to my representative.
S3.think: Privately I think it's tight but doable. If I've moved into running the machines by 63, I might hang on till my pension, or face only a short gap.
S3.do: Joins the trial crew once robots are proven and gets qualified on them in the first couple of years. Does a budget with his partner, saves monthly, pays off the car and pushes for a pension bridge for over-60s.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to act, like climbing in bad weather instead of falling.
S3.quote: The two-year one felt like falling; this feels like climbing in bad weather.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him room to use his usual method of waiting for proof, then moving. He admits they've never done a household budget. His advice to his sons not to copy his caution was a striking bit of self-awareness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we can handle, if we plan. I'd tell the union we should be negotiating now for the next generation, not just for us. I'd be the steady voice at the branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm all right in this one. I'd be retired before it fully lands, and there'd be time to see the machines prove themselves. I'd be more worried for Mateo and Tomas than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and learn the new kit as it shows up, the way I did with drones. I'd keep chipping away at savings and try for that instructor role. Mostly I'd push the union to build a training path for the young guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sad, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 68 by then. Would you even still be working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd be gone at 65, God willing, sooner if the knees decide. With ten years I'd have time to finish properly and hand over to someone. That's what I want, to hand over properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the towers themselves? Would you miss anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The view, sixty metres up at sunrise, with the reservoir like glass. A robot won't care about that. But I wouldn't wish my knees on anyone, so maybe that's fair.

S4.say: I'd say this is the version we can handle if we plan. I'd tell the union to negotiate now for the next generation, not just for us.
S4.think: Privately I think I'm all right in this one, since I'd be retired before it fully lands. I'd worry more for my son and the young crew than for myself.
S4.do: Carries on working and learns new equipment as it is proven, as he did with drones. Keeps saving a little, tries for the instructor role and pushes the union to build a training path for young workers.
S4.feel: Calm, with a touch of sadness.
S4.quote: The view, sixty metres up at sunrise, with the reservoir like glass. A robot won't care about that.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his retirement comes first and his calm returns. He wants above all to hand over properly. His concern moves to the next generation, which fits his union-minded outlook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be finished at 60 with about four weeks of money and nowhere nearby to go. What would help is income support while people bridge to their pension, and training paid for in work hours, before the machines arrive, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the robots. If it's the public company, then the savings could come back to us as lower bills and decent pensions. If it's some outside firm renting them out, we all lose twice.

headlineQuote: If it's some outside firm renting them out, we all lose twice.
portrait: Rafael Torres is a 58-year-old transmission crew foreman who works the big towers between the dam and the city and loves the quiet sixty metres up. He was against drones until they proved useful, and now he uses AI now and then for manuals and reports. He and his partner Lucia live with about four weeks of savings while helping their younger son through his studies. A plateau or slow change leaves him calm or uneasy, with a plan to learn new kit once it's proven. Fast AGI frightens him because it breaks his wait-for-proof method and would end his career at 60, while five or ten years gives him time to qualify, bridge to his pension and hand over properly.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be out of work at 60 with about four weeks of money and no other transmission work nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Income support to bridge people to their pensions, and training paid for in work hours before the machines arrive.
